newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Libya, Ghana being asked about air ban violation.
newsitem.headline: Libya, Ghana being asked about air ban violation.

text.p: A U.N. sanctions committee decided on Monday to ask Libya and Ghana for explanations of recent flights by a Libyan aircraft from Tripoli to Accra and back in apparent violation of a U.N. air ban, the committee's acting chairman said.

Libya has been subject to mandatory U.N. sanctions since 1992, including a ban on all international flights, for failing to extradite two men wanted by Britain and the United States for the 1988 mid-air bombing of a Pan Am airliner over Lockerbie, Scotland, which killed 270 people.
Libya sent a letter to the Security Council last month saying it no longer considered itself bound by the air embargo after giving permission for an American-piloted balloon to overfly its territory.
A Libyan airliner then flew an official delegation to Accra Jan. 21 and returned to Tripoli.

The Security Council issued a statement at a formal meeting last Wednesday noting the Libyan letter "with concern," calling the flights apparent violations of sanctions and referring the matter to the council committee which monitors the sanctions.

The council also noted the sanctions did not prohibit overflights of Libyan territory, thus rejecting Libya's claim that allowing balloonist Steve Fossett to pass over Libya in the course of an unsuccessful around-the-world attempt meant the sanctions no longer applied.

Sanctions committee vice-chairman Park Soo-Gil of South Korea, who chaired Monday's closed-door meeting, told reporters he had been asked to send letters to the U.N. representatives of Libya and Ghana requesting information about the flights.
He said the letters would be dispatched if no committee members raised any objections to the wording by a noon EST (1700 GMT) Wednesday deadline.

A committee source said the letter to Libya would note that international flights by Libyan-registered aircraft required committee approval. Since none was sought, the flights from Tripoli to Accra and back appeared to be a violation of sanctions and Libya would be asked for an early explanation.
The source said Ghana, which had already provided some information about the flight from Tripoli to Accra, would be asked about the return flight, which was also an apparent violation of sanctions.
